passage: Thursday, after dinner. Maths test came back. I got 14 out of 25 and I was hoping for at least 20. On the bus I kept thinking, I must be stupid 😔. Nitin sat next to me and said he lost marks on fractions too, and I didn't say anything. At home I looked at my paper again. All the fraction word problems are wrong, but the multiplication ones are almost all right. That's not everything, is it? Tomorrow I'll ask Papa to give me five fraction sums to do before school. Maybe Nitin can do them with me. - Varun

qa.q: What score did Varun get in the maths test?
What does Varun think on the bus, and what raises doubt about it at home?
qa.a: On the bus Varun thinks "I must be stupid"; at home Varun sees the multiplication answers are almost all right, which raises the question whether one weak topic is everything.

qa.q: What small step would help Varun with fractions?
qa.a: Doing a few fraction sums each day, as Varun plans to ask Papa for, and checking which fraction problems went wrong 🙂.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Varun's silence on the bus?
qa.a: Nitin, who also lost marks on fractions, may have thought Varun was upset and just wanted company; he may not have known how badly Varun felt.

grounding: Illustrates a child doubting themselves after a low mark and shifting to asking which topic went wrong and how to practise.

passage:
'I'm just stupid,' Shankar said, throwing his maths paper on the bed. 'Fifty-two. Everyone else got seventies.'
Aparna Akka picked it up. 'Stupid? You got the whole geometry section right.'
'So? The total's still rubbish.'
'Look here.' She ran her finger down the page. 'You lost almost all your marks in one place. Word problems.'
He leaned over, sniffing. 'I always get confused about what they're asking.'
'That's one topic. Not your whole brain.'
'Feels like my whole brain.'
'I know.' She sat down beside him. 'What if we do three word problems every evening this week? I'll read them aloud with you first.'
Shankar wiped his nose on his sleeve. 'Only three?'
'Only three. If it doesn't help, you can complain all you like.' He laughed despite himself.

qa.q: Which section did Shankar get fully right?
How did Shankar feel when he threw the paper on the bed?
qa.a: Ashamed and defeated, calling himself stupid because others got higher marks.

qa.q: What wiser way of looking at the result did Aparna Akka show?
qa.a: Finding the one topic where the marks were lost, word problems, and practising three a day.

qa.q: How does Aparna Akka see Shankar's result?
qa.a: As trouble with one topic, not proof that he is stupid.

grounding: A boy who calls himself stupid over a low mark is helped by his sister to find the one topic to practise.

passage: When I got my English paper back in Class 6, I saw 38 out of 80 and wanted to crawl into a hole. I'm Farhan. I told myself I was the dumbest person in the whole school. I didn't go out for recess; I sat in the toilets reading the red marks over and over. My friend Ujjwal found me. 'You're not dumb. You beat me in science,' he said. That helped a little. Then I made myself actually look at the paper, not just the total. Most of the red was in one place: tenses. Past, present, all mixed up. That wasn't my whole brain. That was one thing. I asked Ma'am for extra worksheets on tenses. By the half-yearly, I had 61. Still not the top. But not a hole either.

qa.a: In the toilets, reading the red marks.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel on seeing 38 out of 80?
qa.a: Ashamed and crushed, wanting to crawl into a hole and calling Farhan the dumbest person in school.

qa.q: What wiser step did Farhan take after the first shock?
qa.a: Looking at where the marks were lost, tenses, and asking Ma'am for extra worksheets.
As clever, since Farhan beat Ujjwal in science, not dumb at all.

grounding: A child ashamed of a low mark learns to look at which topic went wrong and practise it, instead of judging the whole self.
